turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, doctor. Thanks for seeing me. Um, well, I guess what finally pushed me to come in is that I just can’t seem to organize all the moving parts anymore. 

Between my patent notes at work, workshop prep, team decisions... and gallery deadlines. I do this interactive software art thing on the side, and getting the code to run on these little microcontrollers for the gallery is—well, actually, the gallery owner is this guy I went to grad school with. He used to be in software too, but then he bought this old warehouse downtown. It's got these massive windows, really beautiful natural light, but the heating bill must be absolutely insane in the winter. I keep telling him he needs to insulate the roof, but he says it ruins the industrial aesthetic. I mean, you can see your breath in there in January. 

But anyway, uh... where was I? Right, the moving parts. I just can't organize them. I have all these things going on—the patents, the gallery, the team stuff—and I just end up starting whatever is loudest instead of what actually matters. Like, whoever is pinging me the most gets my attention, and the really important stuff just falls through the cracks.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient explicitly states they have difficulty organizing the moving parts of their various projects and tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, noting that whoever is 'pinging' them the most gets their attention.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, going on a long, unrelated tangent about a gallery owner's warehouse and heating bill before losing their train of thought.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been noticing this difficulty with organizing things and prioritizing—is this something that's been going on for most of your life, or is it something more recent that's developed over the past few months or years?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let me think... It hasn't been my whole life, no. I mean, I've always been a bit scattered, but it really became a huge issue about a year and a month ago. That's when I won this award for a piece I did—it was this really cool installation that reacted to the ambient noise in the room, using these tiny microphones I soldered myself. I actually burned my thumb pretty bad on the soldering iron, still have a little scar right here. I had to use this special silver solder because the connections needed to be super conductive, and you wouldn't believe how hard it is to find good silver solder locally anymore. All the electronics shops I used to go to have closed down. There used to be this great one on 4th Street, run by this guy who knew everything about vintage capacitors. I bought a box of old Soviet vacuum tubes from him once, just because they looked cool. 

But, right, the award. Because of that award, my company decided I should be leading more of these coordination-heavy projects, dealing with the patents and the team decisions. And that's when everything just started falling apart on me.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient confirms that taking on coordination-heavy projects caused everything to start 'falling apart,' indicating difficulty organizing tasks.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts, going on a long tangent about soldering, scars, and electronics shops before returning to the main topic.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned you've always been a bit scattered—when you were younger, say in school or early work, did teachers or supervisors ever comment that you had trouble paying attention, or that you'd jump from task to task, or start things without finishing them?
turns.patient_response:
Well, yeah, actually... looking back, it was definitely there when I was a kid, too. I remember in grade school, my report cards always said the exact same thing. Like, "He's bright, but he daydreams constantly." I used to just stare out the window during math. There was this big oak tree outside my third-grade classroom, and I'd watch the squirrels chasing each other around the trunk. I actually tried to build a squirrel feeder once out of some scrap wood my dad had in the garage. He had this massive collection of power tools he never let me touch, mostly Craftsman stuff from the 80s. They were built like tanks back then, not like the cheap plastic ones you buy now that break after a year. I bought a drill recently that literally smoked the first time I used it on a piece of drywall. 

Anyway... yeah, school. I'd do the homework, right? I'd actually finish the assignments, but then I'd just... forget to turn them in. Or I'd lose my homework folders entirely. My mom used to buy me those Trapper Keepers, the ones with the cool neon designs? I had one with a laser grid and a sports car on it, but the velcro always wore out so fast, and then all your papers would just spill everywhere in your backpack. It was a disaster. So yeah, long before I was even a teenager, I was already losing track of things and forgetting to hand in work I'd already done.

symptom_reasoning.S002: Patient reports constantly daydreaming and staring out the window during math class, indicating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S004: Patient notes he would fail to fully complete his schoolwork duties because he would forget to turn the assignments in.
symptom_reasoning.S007: Patient explicitly mentions losing his homework folders entirely and generally losing track of things.
symptom_reasoning.S008: Patient describes being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as watching squirrels outside the window during class.
symptom_reasoning.S021: Patient demonstrates tangential speech, drifting into unrelated topics about squirrel feeders, his dad's power tools, and a broken drill before returning to the main topic.

turns.doctor_question: Over the past year or so, have you had any periods where you felt unusually energetic, needed much less sleep than normal, or felt like your mood was elevated or expansive for several days at a time?
turns.patient_response:
Unusually energetic? No, not really. I mean, I don't think I've ever had anything like that where I just didn't need sleep. If anything, I'm usually exhausted by the end of the day. I do have nights where I stay up late, but that's just because I get sucked into whatever I'm doing. Like last week, I was trying to fix this bug in the code for the gallery installation, and I ended up going down this massive rabbit hole on GitHub. I found this guy's repository from like, 2015, who was trying to do the exact same thing with the audio processing, but he was using a completely different programming language. It was written in Rust, which I've been meaning to learn. Everyone says Rust is the future because of how it handles memory safety, which is always the biggest headache when you're dealing with C++. I remember back in grad school, I had this professor who was absolutely obsessed with C++. He made us write our own memory allocators from scratch for the final project. Half the class failed because their code just kept leaking memory. He was a tough grader, but he drove this incredible vintage Porsche to campus every day. It was this deep, forest green color. I've always wanted a car like that, but honestly, where I live now, the parking situation is just a nightmare. You have to have a residential permit, and even then, people just leave their cars on the street for weeks. 

But, uh, what were you asking? Oh, right, sleep and energy. Yeah, no, I definitely need my sleep. If I don't get at least seven hours, I'm completely useless the next day. I've never had a time where I felt super energetic for days on end without sleeping.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from coding to a grad school professor, a vintage Porsche, and parking problems before forgetting the original question.
symptom_reasoning.S034: The patient explicitly denies having periods where they felt unusually energetic.
symptom_reasoning.S036: The patient explicitly denies ever experiencing a decreased need for sleep, noting they require at least seven hours to function.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting down trying to focus on work, do you find yourself fidgeting a lot, tapping your fingers or feet, or feeling restless like you need to move around?
turns.patient_response:
Well, fidgeting... I mean, yeah, I guess I do. Especially on those really long design calls. I just get this... this pressure building up inside my body, like I absolutely have to get up. So I end up pacing all around my office, or I'll keep shifting from chair to chair, even when I'm really trying to look like I'm focused on the screen. I actually bought one of those standing desks a while back, thinking it would help. It's one of those motorized ones, you know? The ones where you press a button and it whirs up and down. But the motor on it is so loud. It sounds like a blender grinding ice. I got it from this startup company that was running a huge Kickstarter campaign. They promised all these smart features, like an app that tracks how long you stand, but the app never actually worked right. It would constantly disconnect from the Bluetooth. Bluetooth is just the worst technology, isn't it? I mean, it's been around for decades and it still barely works half the time. I was trying to connect my headphones to my TV the other night to watch this documentary about deep-sea exploration—which was fascinating, by the way, they found these hydrothermal vents that have entire ecosystems living off the chemicals—and the headphones just refused to pair. I must have restarted the TV three times. 

But yeah, on those calls, I'm definitely restless. I just can't stay still for that long.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient confirms fidgeting and describes constantly shifting from chair to chair.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient describes getting up to pace around the office during design calls when they are expected to remain seated and focused on the screen.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient explicitly describes feeling a pressure building up inside their body and states they are 'definitely restless.'
symptom_reasoning.S015: The patient talks excessively, providing a very long response filled with unnecessary details.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the topic of restlessness to standing desks, Kickstarter, Bluetooth issues, and a deep-sea documentary.

turns.doctor_question: When you're in conversations with other people—like in meetings or just talking with friends—do you find yourself interrupting them, or blurting things out before they finish what they're saying?
turns.patient_response:
Interrupting? No, I don't think so. If anything, I'm usually the quiet one in those meetings. I just kind of hang back and let everyone else talk. Especially now that we use Microsoft Teams for everything with the remote developers. It's so hard to jump into a conversation on there anyway because of the audio lag, you know? Plus, there's always someone who forgets to mute their microphone. 

Just last week we had this big architecture review, and the lead engineer's dog was barking non-stop in the background. It sounded exactly like a beagle. I actually really love beagles. My aunt had one when I was a kid named Barnaby, and he was a total escape artist. He dug this massive hole under her chain-link fence and ended up three streets over at a local butcher shop. The butcher actually gave him a huge marrow bone, so of course, Barnaby tried to dig out and go back there every single day after that. 

I've actually been thinking about getting a dog recently, maybe a rescue, but the adoption applications are just completely out of control these days. They want your whole life story, they want to do a home inspection, check three personal references... honestly, it's harder than getting a security clearance. I had to get a clearance once for a government contract job right out of grad school, and the federal investigator literally went and interviewed my neighbors. My neighbor at the time was this retired guy who restored antique radios in his garage. He had hundreds of them, all stacked up to the ceiling... but yeah, I don't really blurt things out. I mostly just listen.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient's response exhibits significant tangentiality, drifting from work meetings to a dog, a butcher shop, adoption applications, security clearances, and antique radios before returning to the question.
symptom_reasoning.S016: The patient explicitly denies blurting things out, stating they mostly just listen.
symptom_reasoning.S018: The patient explicitly denies interrupting others, noting they are usually the quiet one in meetings.

turns.doctor_question: When you're working on something that requires sustained focus—like writing code or reviewing those patent documents—how long can you typically stay focused on that one task before your mind starts wandering to something else?
turns.patient_response:
Well, sustained focus... it really depends, but honestly, not very long at all. If I'm trying to write code or read through those dense documents, I'd say maybe... I don't know, ten, fifteen minutes? And that's if I'm really trying. Because the second something happens—like if Slack pings, or one of those browser notifications flashes up in the corner of the screen, or even if I just get a random visual idea for an installation—I completely lose the thread of what I was doing. I'll just abandon the code and spend twenty minutes going down some totally unrelated design rabbit hole. 

Speaking of Slack, they just pushed this new update that completely changed the layout of the sidebar, and it is driving everyone on my team crazy. They grouped all the direct messages into this weird collapsible menu, so now you have to click twice just to see if someone replied to you. It's terrible UI design. I don't understand why these tech companies feel the need to constantly redesign things that are already working perfectly fine. It's like when Apple removed the headphone jack. I am still annoyed about that. I have this amazing pair of wired Sennheiser headphones that I bought years ago. They have this incredibly flat frequency response, which is perfect for mixing audio for the gallery spaces. You really need a flat response so the bass doesn't get muddy when it's played through those massive PA systems. The last gallery we worked with had these vintage JBL speakers from the 1970s mounted to the ceiling, and the acoustic reflections in that room were just... well, they were a nightmare to EQ. 

But yeah, focus. It's bad. One little distraction and I'm off on something completely different for half an hour before I even realize I stopped coding.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly states they have difficulty sustaining focus on tasks like coding or reading documents, lasting only 10 to 15 minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily derailed from their work by extraneous stimuli (Slack pings, browser notifications) and unrelated internal thoughts (visual ideas).

turns.doctor_question: When you think back to elementary school, before that award and the promotion at work—before age 12—were you already having trouble with attention and organization, or did those problems really start later?
turns.patient_response:
Elementary school... yeah, looking back, it was definitely there in grade school too. I remember my mom kept all these old report cards in a box, and my teachers would always write the exact same thing: that I was a bright kid, but I daydreamed constantly. I used to just stare out the window at the playground. They had this huge metal slide, one of those old, incredibly dangerous ones that would get blistering hot in the summer. You really don't see those anymore. Now all the playgrounds have that soft, bouncy flooring made out of recycled tires. Which is great for safety, I guess, but I read this article recently saying those shredded tires can leach weird chemicals into the ground when they heat up in the sun. It makes you wonder about the long-term environmental impact of all these "green" recycling initiatives, you know? Like, are we just moving the toxic materials from a landfill directly to a kindergarten playground? 

But anyway, yeah, school. Even long before I was a teenager, I was always losing my homework folders. Or the worst part was, I'd actually do the work—I'd sit there and finish the whole assignment at my kitchen table—and then I'd just completely forget to turn it in. The teacher would ask for it, and I'd realize it was crammed at the bottom of my backpack, all crumpled up under my gym clothes. 

My parents tried everything. My dad bought me one of those Trapper Keepers to try and keep me organized. Remember those? Mine had this crazy neon laser grid with a futuristic sports car on the front. I loved that thing, but the velcro on the main flap wore out so fast. Velcro is actually such a brilliant invention, though. It was invented by this Swiss engineer who noticed how burrs stuck to his dog's fur after a walk in the Alps. He actually put the burrs under a microscope to see the tiny hooks. It's amazing how much of our modern engineering is just biomimicry—just copying things nature already perfected millions of years ago. Like how the Japanese bullet trains were modeled after the beak of a kingfisher bird to stop the sonic boom when they exit tunnels... 

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right, before I was 12. Yeah, the daydreaming and losing the folders and all that... it was definitely happening way back then.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient reports they 'daydreamed constantly' and would stare out the window instead of paying attention in class.
symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient confirms having trouble with organization, noting their papers were crumpled in their backpack and their parents bought a Trapper Keeper to help them stay organized.
symptom_reasoning.S007: The patient explicitly states that they were 'always losing my homework folders.'
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient demonstrates distractibility by unrelated thoughts during the interview, losing their train of thought and having to ask what they were talking about.
symptom_reasoning.S009: The patient describes being forgetful in daily school activities, specifically completely forgetting to turn in homework assignments they had already finished.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits marked tangentiality in their speech, drifting into long, unrelated tangents about playground tires, toxic chemicals, velcro, and bullet trains.
